slides.0.title: Plains, an estuary and the Atlantic: geography and climate
slides.0.subtitle: Between 30° and 35° south, a wine country without mountains
slides.1.title: Between 30° and 35° south
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Where it is
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Uruguay lies between about 30° and 35° south. The Río de la Plata estuary is to the south, the Atlantic to the east, the Uruguay River and Argentina to the west, and Brazil to the north
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The land
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The land is low and rolling, mostly gentle hills and plains, with nothing like the Andes. Some vineyards at Cerro Chapeu in Rivera, in the north, sit at about 220 metres, which counts as high here
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The vineyards are in the south
slides.1.highlights.2.content: In 2025 about two thirds of the registered area was in Canelones. With Montevideo and San José, the southern metropolitan coast holds most of the vineyards
slides.1.content: Unlike Argentina and Chile, Uruguayan wine is a story of plains and water.
slides.2.title: The estuary and the Atlantic
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Two bodies of water
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Río de la Plata and the Atlantic temper the south. A 2025 study by Udelar and the University of Rennes 2 found the south-east coast still in a cooler heat class
slides.2.highlights.1.title: A heat gradient
slides.2.highlights.1.content: On 1994–2023 data the Huglin index averages about 2374 nationally. The north now falls entirely in the warmest class, HI5, while the south-east coast remains in the cooler HI3
slides.2.highlights.2.title: A gap in timing
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Modelled for Tannat, flowering and ripening in the north come about two to three weeks earlier than in the south-east: flowering runs from mid-November in the north to late November in the south
slides.2.content: It gets cooler from north to south and from inland towards the Atlantic.
slides.3.title: Rain and vintage variation
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Rain in the growing season
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Rain in the growing season, September to March, averages about 751 mm: about 600 mm in the south and 900 mm in the north. This is very different from a Mediterranean climate with dry summers
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Wet years
slides.3.highlights.1.content: 2024, an El Niño year, was wet. The study notes that drought risk fell but other hazards such as fungal disease rose
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Hot, dry years
slides.3.highlights.2.content: 2023, a La Niña year, was hot and dry. The Huglin index rose to about 2543 and 80% of the country fell in the hottest class, HI5
slides.3.content: To read a Uruguayan vintage, first ask whether it was an El Niño or a La Niña year.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Roughly what latitude does Uruguay span?
The Río de la Plata is to the south and the Atlantic to the east.
On 1994–2023 data, which area remains in the cooler HI3 class?
B. The north-west along the Uruguay River
C. None: the whole country is now HI5
D. The south-east coast, tempered by the estuary and the Atlantic
The north is now entirely HI5.
How does growing-season rain (September to March) differ between north and south?
C. More in the north (about 900 mm against 600 mm)
D. It hardly rains in the growing season
The national average is about 751 mm.
